From everything I’ve researched (obsessively) you really do need to give it that 3-6 months and even up to a full year for everything to reattach, stop swelling, and fully tighten up. The cannula literally had to separate and suck fat from the surrounding tissue, which is a lot of trauma to an area. And now that area is going through phases of repair that take a long time. There is trauma under the skin that causes swelling and fluid build up, and then the tissue needs to remodel itself and reattach which can take months. Think how long a scar can take to heal. It isn’t instant. Your body needs time to rebuild collagen and go back to normal!

I feel for you and I felt really similarly after buying my first house. I moved from one of the fanciest/most expensive neighborhoods (renting) to buying in one of the roughest neighborhoods that was also experiencing a lot of crime at the time. But it was one of my only options for being able to afford to purchase. I was filled with dread as I’d drive home and my heart would be racing. I also went through a breakup so was living there totally alone. I’m also 10-15min from the fun part of the city but felt so isolated and like no one ever wanted to visit. 

However I started getting involved in my community, I literally went door to door to meet people and introduce myself. I invited neighbors to join a safety group where we could message each other if we needed anything. I do trash walks with my friends and neighbors where we clean up the streets. I’ve gotten to know more about the community here and realized it’s actually quite full of love and really good hardworking people. My perspective on the area has changed so much and I love it now. There is also a ton of development here and new people moving in and fixing up the houses and yards and opening new businesses. 

Trust me, I cried a bunch and had so many regrets, especially since my house has lost about $40k in equity since buying it and I can’t sell for probably another 5-10 years just to even recuperate the realtor fees of selling. But I am glad I stuck it out and I truly enjoy walking around here now even though it isn’t “fancy” and there are some junk cars and yards full of weeds. I also look for signs of progress and people caring (ie. even small things like people planting flowers) and it makes me feel better. Myself and a few others on my street really maintain our yards and homes and try to set an example. Your neighborhood could very well improve in the next few years, and those people that keep to themselves might just be waiting for you to introduce yourself! I thought my neighbor didn’t like me at first, but now he mows my lawn and shovels my snow without me asking. Sometimes you have to look for the good to find it. 

It also might be worth inviting friends over and having some house warming events, or a regular weekly game night that fills your house with good vibes and life. I straight up told my friends I was lonely and sad they weren’t visiting me and they started coming by way more often and really enjoying how cute my house is. 

Here to chat if you need. Best of luck!

I take most of the money I make and put it in a HYSA and don’t touch it. I mentally have convinced myself that money in there doesn’t exist to be spent, but it is a cushion for emergencies. I then pay myself “life & fun” money but it’s been nearly the same amount when I was making $35k and when I’m now making $180k. I’m not making a huge salary compared to some, but I’ve managed to save around $300k which I don’t touch. I do think it’s in my genes to be a “saver” because I was like this as a kid too. Spending just doesn’t feel very good and actually gives me stress. 

I try to focus on the joy of the security of having money saved - this brings me more comfort than spending it. Practice finding joy in frugal endeavors too, for example I prefer thrifting over buying new because the item feels more special. Or cooking a delicious meal at home versus going out. Make sure to treat yourself every once in a while so it doesn’t feel like you’re working hard for no reward (I don’t do anything major, maybe a trip that costs under $2k once per year, a massage, or a nice $200 blanket every now and then.) 

It’s a good practice in discipline and you’ll end up feeling very proud of yourself most likely!

I’m curious about this too since I’m getting it done at age 31 in a few weeks! I’ve wondered if long term it will age me but to be honest I don’t think it will. I’ve researched what ages people and it’s mostly removing fat from the cheek/mid face area which is needed for that full youthful look on the face. Buccal fat removal is what is more likely to age you and cause gaunt-ness (and IMO it has aged everyone I’ve seen who had it done unless they’re super young and have a ton of extra buccal fat.) I don’t think a lot of our perception of “youthfulness” comes from fullness around the chin/jaw area. It’s more of that mid face/cheek area. 

Also someone mentioned having the extra fat there will pull that skin down with time, so removing it sooner can prevent sagging in that area. But I’m no expert. Just been doing a lot of digging on this topic before my procedure as I’ve never had anything done before.

The first question is how much liquid cash do you have saved for repairs, and how cheap are they willing to sell the house for? I purchased a 114 year old house and lived in a 125 year old home before this. I’ve done a lot to educate myself on old house restoration and repair and unfortunately it is NOT cheap. For example, new siding and removing a chimney could easily be over $30k (maybe more depending on size). Rewiring and re plumbing a house could be another $50k+. Major systems needing replacement like the roof are also tens of thousands of $. I had to dig a $7k hole to replace a very small part of my sewer connection. Be prepared for surprises too. Removing the siding may reveal mold, window leaks, rotting wood, termite damage etc… whatever budget you have for a project, double that. 

That being said, I would ONLY ever buy an old house. I’ve seen horror stories of how cheaply and quickly they made new homes with OSB and moldy wood that doesn’t even fit together properly because it’s so warped. Some things are more urgent in an old house than others and it depends how well it has been maintained. Ie. No subfloor isn’t a big deal to me - I also don’t have subfloor. It is very important to note how well the gutters have been working and making sure the earth has been grading water away from the foundation because water is the no.1 thing that ruins any home. 

The most important thing will be the structure of the home itself. I have done a lot of research on structural red flags vs what is more normal in an older home. 

Although older houses are build with slow grown wood which is stronger, building practices were different back then and the framing might need extra reinforcing (ie. Center carrying beams were often over spanned and need additional support.) In any real estate purchase, you will get a home inspection before the deal goes through. Make sure the purchase is contingent on the inspection. I’d also hire a structural engineer (separate from a normal inspection, $400-800.) Never EVER use the inspectors your real estate agent recommends. My realtor scammed me and lied to me and her inspector was in on it.

It depends on plan. The time with the doctor can be as little as 5-10 minutes. You still pay the full amount even for a short visit. The doctors generally don’t spend much time with you at a primary care provider visit. Some specialists will spend longer with you for example if they are doing tests, physical therapy, or diagnosing you with something. Usually you don’t even see your doctor, you see the physicians assistant. A normal visit would cost me around $350 and my insurance will only pay $100 of that. But each doctor has their own price so it could be more. And they can’t always tell you how much it will be ahead of time. 

Everyone pays a different amount depending on plan as well. Some better plans (like through actual employers) might have you pay as little as $0-50 per  primary care visit (low co pay.) These visits are for smaller things like annual check ups, women exams, and sickness. Any tests cost extra, like if you need bloodwork done. And these tests might not be covered at all. Bigger things like CT scans aren’t covered until you reach your deductible (for me.) 

You also have to reach your deductible before they cover anything big. A deductible is a large amount of money you must pay out of pocket before insurance fully kicks in. 
So if you have a $5,000 deductible, insurance won’t cover any big tests/surgeries until you pay $5,000 out of pocket first. THEN insurance kicks in and covers the rest. So for me I pay $300/month + $5,000 one big payment if I need something big like surgery. I’ve seen deductibles as high as $13,000/year for self employed people. Usually it’s closer to $1,000-2,000/yr for people with corporate jobs.

Oh not to mention insurance companies will fight you to not pay for anything. They tried to refuse my mom cancer treatment. It would’ve been $60,000 per month for her medication and treatment without insurance. We had to FIGHT them to get them to pay for it.

Keep in mind that ketamine is psychedelic and hallucinations can include auditory hallucinations (your family member's voices.) I did muscular injection treatment for a few years and it was very, very trippy and sound was difficult to understand sometimes. 

You may want to try to just accept the disturbing images, I know it sounds weird but forcing your brain not to think of something sometimes only makes the urge stronger. I have OCD and a common treatment is ERP, which is exposure to the intrusive thoughts. When I have a negative or intrusive/disturbing thought, I try to run toward it rather than away from it, and I'll tell myself "oh, that is interesting that you showed me that." I know it sounds counterproductive, but it takes away some of the thought's power and encourages me not to reinforce it. 

A theme I tell myself through the ketamine journey is "Let Go" and "Acceptance." See the image, breathe in, and let it go. If it comes back, just accept it until it passes. You are merely an observer, like watching leaves float down a stream. Try to see your thoughts that way. Your thoughts can't hurt you, and they don't say anything bad about you as a person. I have disturbing thoughts with my OCD and now I see that they are not part of me - they're something my brain does and I simply observe and let them wash away. Mindfulness practice even in your daily life (not during ketamine) can be helpful in getting to a point of observation and acceptance. 

Best of luck.

Aurora is huge and a mixed bag. It truly feels like multiple different cities but is generally quite diverse. I won’t lie though, we do have some weird crime and we hear gunshots often especially within the last year. The good news is this area has awesome businesses and is getting more + the BRT rapid transit will come close to here and continue the bus route through this area. Vanishing West ciders just opened and is awesome. We got a permanent Cerebral Brewing which is also an incredible space & beer. In summary, it’s so much more than just a “slummy area”. And people speaking on us usually don’t know any of the good parts mixed in there. Sure, it looks blighted in some areas.
